prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Jay, Wright

outputs.L1:
For Jay Wright

My old man took me to the Fulton Fish Market.  
We walked around in the guts and the scales.  
My old man showed me a dead fish,  
its eyes like throat spit.

He said, “You hungry, boy?”  
I said, “No, not yet.”

My old man showed me how to pick through the leavings.  
He said people throw away fish that are not rotten.  
We scaled them on our knees.

Back uptown on Lenox,  
we sold five fish  
and kept one for the pot.

My old man bought a bottle of wine.  
He said, “Boy, build me a fire out in the lot.”

A backyard cat climbed up my leg for fish.  
I made a fire in the ash can.  
My old man came when he smelled the fish.  
Frank Williams was with him;  
they had wine.

My old man said, “The boy caught the big one.”  
He told a big lie  
and slapped me on the head.

I gave the guts to the cat  
and took myself some wine.

We walked around the sparks  
as if we were in hell.  
My old man was laughing  
and coughing up wine.

He said, “You hungry, boy?”  
I said, “No, not yet.”

The next time I went to the Fulton Fish Market,  
the first thing I did  
was take a long drink of wine.
outputs.L2:
For Jay Wright

My father took me down to the Fulton Fish Market. We moved among the fish remains—slime, scales, and innards everywhere. He pointed to a dead fish with eyes cloudy and wet, like spit from a throat, and asked, “You hungry, boy?”

I told him, “No, not yet.”

He taught me how to sort through what others had left behind, explaining that people tossed out fish even when they were still good. We cleaned them on our knees. Later, back uptown on Lenox, we sold five of the fish and saved one to cook.

My father bought a bottle of wine. Then he told me, “Boy, make me a fire out in the lot.”

A backyard cat clawed up my leg, wanting fish. I built the fire inside an ash can. When the smell of cooking fish rose, my father came over with Frank Williams. They had wine with them.

My father said, “The boy caught the big one,” making up a grand story, and smacked me on the head. I gave the fish guts to the cat and took a drink of wine for myself.

We circled the flying sparks as if we were moving through hell. My father laughed and coughed wine back up. Again he asked, “You hungry, boy?”

I said, “No, not yet.”

The next time I went to the Fulton Fish Market, the first thing I did was take a deep drink of wine.
outputs.L3:
The speaker’s father takes him to the Fulton Fish Market, where he teaches him how to search through the discarded fish and recognize which ones are still usable. This lesson is not simply about food; it is about survival. The father shows the speaker how to look carefully, how to judge what can still be eaten, and how to make use of what others have thrown away.

After they find six usable fish, they take them uptown to Lenox Avenue. There, they sell five of the fish and keep one for themselves. The sale gives them a little money, while the remaining fish becomes their meal. This moment shows how closely hunger and earning money are connected in their lives: even discarded food can become both income and dinner.

With the money from the fish, the father buys wine. He then tells the speaker to build a fire in the lot so they can cook the fish they have saved. The scene becomes a mixture of necessity and celebration. They are still poor and hungry, but they have managed to find food, sell some of it, and create a small meal for themselves.

As the father drinks and laughs with Frank Williams, he begins to exaggerate the speaker’s role in catching the fish. He turns the boy’s simple work at the market into a larger, more heroic story. Through his joking and boasting, the father reshapes the experience, making it sound as if the speaker had been actively involved in catching the fish rather than merely helping to recover what had been discarded.

By the end, the experience connects hunger, survival, storytelling, and wine. The speaker learns that wine is part of the ritual surrounding hardship: it accompanies the search for food, the selling of fish, the cooking in the lot, and the father’s laughter and exaggeration. On the speaker’s next trip to the market, this connection has already taken hold. Before searching for fish, he drinks wine first, showing how deeply the lesson has become tied to his understanding of survival.
outputs.L4:
The narrative presents poverty not as an abstraction but as a daily, physical experience: the smell of fish, the cold of the market, the weight of crates, the sting of hunger, and the hard knowledge that survival often depends on what others throw away. At Fulton Fish Market, the father and son move through the remains of commerce, searching among discarded fish and scraps for anything that can still be used. What has been rejected by buyers and workers becomes, for them, a possible meal, a small source of money, kindling for fire, or part of a repeated family ritual. The market is both a place of humiliation and resourcefulness, where waste is transformed into sustenance through labor, instinct, and necessity.

At the center of the text is the relationship between the father and the boy. The father teaches his son how to survive in a world that offers them very little. He shows him where to look, what to take, how to carry himself, and how to turn refuse into something valuable. These lessons are practical, but they are also emotional and moral. The boy learns that hunger requires toughness, that poverty demands improvisation, and that shame must often be hidden behind bravado. His father’s confidence, roughness, and rituals give the experience a kind of dignity, even as the conditions themselves reveal deep deprivation.

Yet the father’s lessons are not purely heroic. Alongside resilience, the boy also absorbs hardship, danger, and damage. Alcohol, boasting, exhaustion, and the constant struggle for food shape the atmosphere of the narrative. The father’s strength is inseparable from his wounds, and the boy’s admiration is mixed with fear and awareness. What is being passed down is not only a method of survival but also a burden: a way of living formed by scarcity, pride, and pain.

The text therefore turns an act of scavenging into a larger meditation on inheritance. Poverty teaches the boy ingenuity, endurance, and closeness to his father, but it also exposes him to suffering and instability. The discarded fish become symbols of a life made from leftovers, a life in which nothing can be wasted because there is never enough. Through vivid sensory detail and the intimate bond between father and son, the narrative shows how deprivation can create rituals of strength while also leaving lasting scars.

Wright’s coaching style emphasized strong fundamentals, unselfish play, and a calm but confident approach. He was admired not only for winning games, but also for developing players into leaders on and off the court. His teams were known for their smart decision-making, excellent shooting, and commitment to defense.

Beyond basketball, Jay Wright became known for his professionalism and character. His influence continues to be felt in the sport, and his legacy remains an important part of college basketball history.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a gritty free-verse poem dedicated to Jay Wright about a boy and his father going to the Fulton Fish Market, using Black vernacular, fish imagery, wine, hunger, and a recurring line “you hongry boy?”
counterfactuals.output:
**At Fulton Before the Sun**  
*for Jay Wright*

before morning got its shoes on  
my old man shook me loose from sleep—  
his hand rough as a dock rope,  
his breath carrying last night’s wine  
and whatever prayer a poor man swallows  
when the rent come due.

“you hongry boy?”

he said it like hunger was my name,  
like I was born with a hole in me  
big enough to keep the river moving.

we took the train down  
where the city still had fish-blood  
under its fingernails,  
where men in rubber boots  
dragged the sea by its silver ankles  
across the concrete.

Fulton was awake already,  
cussing and shining—  
ice cracked like teeth,  
bluefish stiff as trouble,  
flounder flat with knowing,  
stripers stacked like knives  
somebody forgot to hide.

my father walked through it  
like he owned nothing  
and still belonged to everything.

“you hongry boy?”

I was.  
hongry for bread,  
for his hand to stay on my shoulder,  
for the world to stop selling  
what it had killed.

he bought no fish at first.  
just looked.  
nodded at the men  
with scales on their sleeves,  
men who laughed from the gut  
and spat into the gutter  
like spitting could keep death back.

somebody passed him a bottle—  
cheap red, no label left,  
warm from a coat pocket.  
he took a pull  
and the morning opened its dark mouth.

I watched his throat work.  
watched him hand it back  
like communion was a debt  
between broke men.

“you hongry boy?”

the fish stared up  
with moon-eyes,  
each one asking  
what kind of God  
make a body shine best  
after it’s dead.

my father picked through whiting,  
haggled low,  
voice gravel and smoke.

“man, don’t play me—  
I got a child here.”

the fishman laughed.  
“everybody got a child here.”

and wasn’t that the truth—  
all us sons of somebody  
standing in the stink,  
waiting to be weighed,  
wrapped, carried home.

my stomach folded in on itself.  
the market smelled like salt,  
diesel, iron,  
old rope, old hurt,  
and that sour wine  
blooming from my father’s coat.

he gave me a look  
soft as a bruise.

“you hongry boy?”

I wanted to say  
I’m hongry for you sober.  
I’m hongry for the light bill paid.  
I’m hongry for Mama not turning  
her face to the wall.

but I just nodded.

he bought a paper sack of fish,  
their tails knocking together  
like small hard bells.  
then we walked back  
through the city’s gray beginning,  
past trucks coughing smoke,  
past men lifting crates  
like lifting was the only psalm  
they ever learned.

my father said,  
“sea give, sea take.  
don’t you forget that.”

but all I could think was  
the sea ain’t give us nothing—  
men went in and took it,  
dragged up hunger by the gills,  
sold it before dawn.

on the train home  
he leaned against the window,  
eyes half shut,  
the sack between his boots  
leaking a thin bright water.

I sat beside him  
holding my own hands,  
smelling fish, wine, winter,  
and the long work  
of being his boy.

“you hongry boy?”

yeah.

I was hongry.

hongry as the market after midnight,  
hongry as a hook,  
hongry as the mouth of every fish  
caught open  
when the world come down.

and my father—  
Lord, my father—  
he was hongry too.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the style of mid-20th-century urban oral storytelling: a father takes his son from Lenox Avenue to the Fulton Fish Market, they salvage fish, cook in a lot, drink wine, and the poem ends with the boy learning to drink first.
counterfactuals.output:
My old man come up Lenox  
with his hat leaning back  
like it knew more weather than he did,  
and he say, Boy,  
don’t let morning catch you sleeping  
when hunger got shoes on.

So we walked.

Past the brownstones sweating coal-smoke,  
past the women shaking rugs out windows,  
past the men in doorways  
talking loud enough to keep warm,  
me half-running beside him  
with my hands in my pockets  
and the city opening its iron mouth.

Down to the market,  
where the river smelled like money gone bad,  
where fish lay silver and stiff  
on beds of ice,  
and men with knives for fingers  
hollered prices at the dawn.

My father knew the back end  
of every honest thing.  
He knew what fell off carts,  
what got bruised,  
what a man could ask for  
without calling it begging.

He said, These here still good.  
Just lost their shine, that’s all.  
Same as folks.

We took whiting,  
a bluefish with one cloudy eye,  
some crabs knocking prayers  
against the bucket,  
and he carried them uptown  
like he had robbed the sea itself.

In a vacant lot off Lenox,  
where weeds grew through brick  
and somebody’s old mattress  
dreamed in the rain,  
my father made a fire  
from orange crates and newspaper.

The smoke climbed up  
between the tenements,  
and the fish hissed in a black pan  
he kept wrapped in a sack.  
Grease popped like small talk.  
Salt came from his coat pocket.  
Pepper too.

Then he pulled the wine out—  
red and cheap and mean—  
and wiped the neck  
with the back of his hand.

I watched him drink.  
I watched his throat learn mercy.  
He looked at me and laughed,  
not soft,  
but close enough.

Boy, he said,  
the world don’t hand you nothing  
but bones.  
You got to learn  
where the meat is.

He passed me the bottle.

I thought a man drank  
after he had eaten,  
after the plate was clean,  
after the hunger  
had been fooled.

But my father shook his head.

First, he said.  
Drink first.

So I did.

And the wine burned down  
like a little red lesson,  
and the fish smoked over the fire,  
and Lenox Avenue leaned in listening  
while I stood there with my father,  
learning how poor men  
bless the day  
before they take from it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a raw narrative poem titled “for Jay Wright” about poverty, masculinity, and survival in Harlem, with an “ole man,” dead fish, cats, an ash-can fire, and repeated dialogue about being hungry.
counterfactuals.output:
# for Jay Wright

Up on 137th  
where the brick sweats black in August  
and winter comes in through the teeth,  
the ole man kept his hands  
deep in the pockets of a coat  
that had forgotten every owner  
before him.

He said,  
“I’m hungry.”

The boy said,  
“Everybody hungry.”

They stood by the fish market  
after closing,  
where the dead fish lay in a crate  
silver-eyed, stiff as bad luck,  
their mouths open  
like they had been asking God  
the wrong question.

Cats came from under cars,  
thin-backed, church-quiet,  
stepping soft around broken glass.  
One cat took a fish head  
and vanished into Harlem  
like it owed somebody money.

The ole man laughed  
without showing joy.

He said,  
“Boy, you hungry?”

The boy said,  
“I said I’m hungry.”

The ole man said,  
“Then stand like a man.”

But the boy had seen men  
stand all day on corners  
with nothing in their stomachs  
but smoke and memory,  
seen men slap women  
because rent was due,  
seen men turn their pockets inside out  
like wounded birds,  
seen men call it pride  
when they would not beg  
and call it weakness  
when they cried in the hallway.

So the boy said nothing.

Down the block  
somebody had lit an ash-can fire,  
orange tongues licking trash,  
warming hands,  
warming lies,  
warming the last blue hour  
before night came down  
with police sirens in its coat.

Men circled the flame  
like old planets,  
passing a bottle,  
passing names of the dead,  
passing silence  
from mouth to mouth.

The ole man held out his palms.

He said,  
“I’m hungry.”

A man by the fire said,  
“Who ain’t?”

Another said,  
“Hungry don’t make you special.”

Another said,  
“Hungry make you mean.”

The boy watched the dead fish  
go pale in the crate,  
watched the cats return  
with their yellow eyes burning,  
watched the ole man straighten his back  
like hunger was a uniform  
he had been issued at birth.

“Listen,” the ole man said,  
“a man survives.”

The boy said,  
“How?”

The ole man looked toward the fire,  
toward the cats,  
toward the fish,  
toward the avenue where buses groaned  
full of people going somewhere  
they did not own.

He said,  
“Any way he can.”

Then he reached into the crate  
and took two dead fish,  
slick with cold,  
wrapped them in yesterday’s news,  
and tucked them under his arm  
like scripture.

The boy said,  
“I’m hungry.”

The ole man said,  
“I know.”

The boy said,  
“I’m hungry.”

The ole man said,  
“Then walk.”

And they walked  
past the ash-can fire,  
past the men pretending  
flame was enough,  
past the cats making a feast  
of what the city threw away,  
past the windows glowing gold  
above rooms they could not enter.

Harlem held them  
the way a fist holds a coin.

The ole man walked slow.  
The boy walked beside him.  
Neither one spoke  
of love.

But when the wind cut hard  
through Lenox Avenue,  
the ole man shifted the fish  
to his other arm  
and put his free hand  
on the boy’s shoulder,

not gentle,  
not soft,  
not fatherly enough  
to be called mercy,

but heavy,  
warm,

alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse piece that sounds like a child remembering his father: Fulton Fish Market, leavings from fish stalls, selling fish uptown, cooking one in a backyard lot, Frank Williams showing up with wine, and a darkly funny ending.
counterfactuals.output:
My father smelled like Fulton Fish Market  
before the sun came up,  
like cold knives,  
wet wood,  
and the ocean after it had been argued with.

He brought home what was left—  
fish with one eye cloudy,  
tails bent like question marks,  
silver bodies nobody uptown wanted  
until he made them want them.

He’d load a crate  
and ride north,  
calling out prices  
like he was singing church songs  
to people in windows  
who leaned down and asked  
if it was fresh.

Fresh, he’d say,  
fresh enough to bite you back.

One evening he kept one for us,  
a big ugly fish  
wrapped in newspaper  
that had already told bad news.

We cooked it in the empty lot  
behind the buildings,  
over wood we weren’t supposed to burn,  
with smoke climbing up the brick  
like it was trying to escape the neighborhood.

Then Frank Williams came around  
with a bottle of wine,  
grinning like he owned half the moon.  
He said,  
I smelled supper from the corner,  
and my father said,  
Then your nose owes me rent.

They drank from paper cups.  
I ate with my fingers.  
The fish was black on one side  
and soft as a secret on the other.

My father laughed that night,  
a big laugh,  
the kind that made adults look younger  
for a second.

Later I asked him  
what kind of fish it was.

He looked at the bones,  
then at Frank,  
then at the empty bottle,  
and said,  
Son, by tomorrow  
we’ll know if it was dinner  
or a murder weapon.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a vernacular poem without punctuation-heavy formatting, dedicated to Jay Wright, where a boy’s father teaches him how to scavenge and sell fish, then they roast one over a trash-can fire and walk around the sparks “like we in hell.”
counterfactuals.output:
For Jay Wright

Daddy say come on boy  
tide done left us something

so we walk the back dock  
where gulls cuss the morning  
and the fish lay silver tired  
in crates behind the market

he show me which ones still good  
eye clear  
gill red  
belly not gone soft with leaving

this one sell  
this one keep  
this one toss back to the cats

I carry a bucket  
near big as my hunger  
Daddy carry two  
and don’t spill nothing

men at the corner laugh  
say yall selling sea ghosts  
Daddy grin and say  
ghost still fry up fine

we get coins  
we get a dollar folded wet  
we get told move along  
we move along

by dark the cold come up mean  
so Daddy turn a trash can holy  
with paper and crate wood  
and one fish laid on wire

grease talk to flame  
smoke get in our shirts  
stars hide behind the overpass

Daddy say eat slow  
bones got a mind of they own

we stand there chewing  
our faces orange then black  
orange then black  
and sparks jump out the barrel  
trying to be heaven

Daddy laugh  
kick his boots round the fire  
I dance behind him

round and round that burning can  
with fish salt on our fingers  
and smoke in our teeth

like we in hell  
but full  
and together
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
